evidence: Canonical reports on the local machine; paths are relative to the evidence root.

highlights.title: Swift MEDIUM recovers correctness at near-equal cost
highlights.text: On eight frozen low-risk coding tasks, one natural attempt each, Swift LOW was accepted on 6 and Swift MEDIUM on all 8, fixing both LOW failures with no new ones. Median wall time was 159.7 s for MEDIUM against 160.1 s for LOW; total wall rose 6.9 %.

highlights.title: MEDIUM is competitive with Scope on matched tasks
highlights.text: On the three tasks with a matched Scope run, MEDIUM's median wall was 139.7 s against 144.9 s, with less observed reasoning time and fewer generated tokens. The Scope sample is historical and small.

highlights.title: Agent latency is model-compute bound
highlights.text: A latency decomposition of six valid coding runs attributed about 95 % of warm task time to native inference. Start-up and tool overhead were minor, so harness tuning has little left to give.

highlights.title: Stable-prefix restore helps first token, not the task
highlights.text: Restoring a 6,144-token task-free prefix saved a median 21.1 s to first token but only 5.65 % of paired task wall time, below the 15 % target. It stays experimental.

highlights.title: Native MTP is worth about 5 % of decode
highlights.text: Across 20 parity-qualified synthetic pairs, adaptive multi-token prediction raised median decode from 30.96 to 32.35 tok/s (+5.34 %). Start-up was measured at 3.3 s to the first request with at most 123 ms left to gain.

highlights.title: NVFP4 expert weights repack exactly; 2 bits is the hard part
highlights.text: The ModelOpt NVFP4 container decodes exactly (E2M1 codes, E4M3 block scales, an FP32 tensor scale). Requantizing 4-bit experts to the 2.25-bit Q2_0 container with a per-block scale search halves the weight error of the standard encoder (0.36 against 0.72 relative RMS).

highlights.title: An upstream conversion path drops the n-gram table's scale
highlights.text: The n-gram embedding table is stored as FP8 values times one BF16 scalar (0.000199). The upstream converter upcasts the shards and loses that scalar, which would make the table about 5,000 times too large. The DwarfStar conversion applies it and refuses to publish unless the decoded magnitude matches.

highlights.title: Cyber runs the full agent stack at 128K
highlights.text: The converted model loads in 22 s cold, decodes at 32 to 36 tok/s with native MTP (output identical with MTP off), describes images through its own projector, and drives the same tools as the other models. Prefilling in 1024-token chunks brings its 128K plan to 50.81 GiB, under the 51.84 GiB GPU working-set limit; a 120,399-token needle test then passed where the 2048-chunk configuration had failed.

highlights.title: The remaining weakness is measurable
highlights.text: On one 8.3K-token agent request sampled 80 times, Cyber ended the turn after a few junk tokens 4 times; Scope and Swift did so 0 times. Temperature 0 is always correct and a min-p floor only halves the rate, which points at the data-free 2-bit expert encoding. A calibrated re-encode from the same source is the planned fix.

highlights.title: Telemetry costs nothing when nobody is watching
highlights.text: The telemetry-capable runtime produces token-identical output to the reference builds for all three models and the same decode speed when no consumer is subscribed (for example 41.0 against 40.9 tok/s on Scope).
